passages.t: Ananias lies to the Holy Spirit
passages.happening:
A man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sells a piece of property. With her full knowledge, he keeps back part of the money for himself and brings the rest and lays it at the apostles' feet, as if it were the whole.

Peter says, “Ananias, how is it that Satan has filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and withhold some of the proceeds from the land?” (verse 3). The land was his own before he sold it, Peter says, and the money was his to use after. “How could you conceive such a deed in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God” (verse 4).

“On hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. And great fear came over all who heard what had happened” (verse 5). The young men wrap up his body, carry him out and bury him.
passages.hearers:
Luke has just told of Barnabas, who sold a field and gave the money (4:36-37). In a community where generous giving was noticed and honoured, Ananias and Sapphira wanted the same honour at less cost. They gave part and said it was all.

Peter is clear about what the sin was. It was not keeping money. Ananias did not have to sell the land, and he did not have to give all of it. The sin was the lie: pretending before God and the church to have given everything. In a world where honour and reputation mattered greatly, they reached for the praise without the gift.

Notice too that Peter says Ananias lied ‘to the Holy Spirit’, and then that he lied ‘to God’. The early church spoke of the Spirit as God himself.

Peter pronounces no curse and lifts no hand. He names the sin, and Ananias falls. The burial is quick, with no time for mourning, and that shows how sudden and shocking it was.
passages.ot:
Many readers compare this story with Achan in the book of Joshua. As Israel began its life in the promised land, Achan “took some of what was set apart” for God and hid it in his tent (Joshua 7:1, 21), and he died for it. Many readers notice that the Greek word for ‘kept back’ in Acts 5:2 is the word the old Greek translation used for Achan's sin. At both beginnings, of Israel in the land and of the church in Jerusalem, a hidden sin threatens God's people at its birth.

The story also recalls the deaths of Nadab and Abihu at the start of Israel's worship (Leviticus 10:1-2), and of Uzzah beside the ark (2 Samuel 6:7).
passages.hard:
This is one of the hardest stories in the New Testament, and Luke does not soften it. A man and his wife die for a lie about money. Readers have always found it troubling, and they should not hide that. Peter was forgiven for denying Jesus; Saul will be forgiven for hunting the church. Why not Ananias?

Readers have understood it in several ways, and these are views, not settled answers. Many see it as a sign at the founding of the church, like Achan at Israel's founding: the holy God is present among his people by his Spirit, and deliberate deceit at the heart of that new community was deadly serious. Some ask whether it was God's direct judgment or the shock of being found out; Luke does not say how Ananias died, only that he fell when he heard Peter's words. Readers also differ on whether Ananias and Sapphira were true believers who lost their lives but not their salvation (compare 1 Corinthians 11:30, where Paul says some believers have died for misusing the Lord's Supper), or people who were never truly part of the church. Most agree that the story is not a pattern for how churches should treat sin, which the rest of the New Testament describes as aimed at restoring the sinner.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And the same chapter offers mercy. Before it ends, Peter tells the council that God has exalted Jesus ‘to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins’ (verse 31).
passages.asks: Ananias did not have to give. He chose to pretend. Ask where you are tempted to look more generous, more holy or more committed than you are. God is not asking for a show. He is asking for the truth, and the truth, confessed, is always met with forgiveness: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9).

passages.happening:
About three hours later Sapphira comes in, not knowing what has happened. Peter asks her whether this is the price “you and your husband got for the land”. She answers yes: “that is the price” (verse 8).

Peter replies, “How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?” And he adds, “Look, the feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also” (verse 9). At once she falls down at his feet and dies, and the young men bury her beside her husband.

“And great fear came over the whole church and all who heard about these events” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Peter gives Sapphira a chance to tell the truth. He asks a plain question. She could have said, ‘No, we kept some back.’ She chose the lie her husband had told. The story is told as a matched pair: the same sin, the same question, the same end.

Husband and wife had agreed together. The plan was shared, and so was its outcome. Sapphira was not punished for her husband's sin, but for her own.

This is the first place the word ‘church’ appears in Acts in most modern Bibles. It translates ekklēsia, an assembly or gathering, the word the Greek Old Testament used for the assembly of Israel. The first time the church is named, it is a people who have just learned that God is holy.

‘Great fear’ is not simple terror. In the Bible, the fear of God is awe at who he is. Luke says it twice, for the church and for everyone who heard.
passages.ot:
‘Test the Spirit of the Lord’ recalls Israel in the wilderness, who tested God again and again. Moses warned, “Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah” (Deuteronomy 6:16).

The fear that came on everyone recalls the Law's words after judgment fell in Israel: “Then all Israel will hear and be afraid” (Deuteronomy 13:11). The point in both is not cruelty, but that God's people learn he is not to be trifled with.
passages.asks: Sapphira was given a second chance to tell the truth and did not take it. Ask whether there is something you have agreed to hide with someone else, in a marriage, a family or a church, and whether there is still time to bring it into the light. And ask what the fear of God means to you: dread, or awe that changes how you live.

passages.t: Signs and wonders, and the sick in the streets
passages.happening:
The apostles do many signs and wonders among the people. The believers meet together in Solomon's Colonnade. Others do not dare join them, yet the people think highly of them, and more and more men and women believe.

People carry the sick into the streets on cots and mats, “so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by” (verse 15). Crowds come from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, “and all of them were healed” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Luke's summary shows two reactions at once. The people respect the believers, but after Ananias and Sapphira, no one joins them lightly. Yet more and more do believe and join. Following Jesus has become serious, and still people come.

Many in the ancient world believed that a holy person's power could reach others by touch, by clothing, even by a shadow. Luke tells what the people did without teaching it as a method. A woman had touched the fringe of Jesus' cloak (Luke 8:44), and later handkerchiefs that had touched Paul were taken to the sick (19:12). In each case it is the Lord who heals, not the cloth or the shadow.

The good news is beginning to move out from the city. People come in from the towns around Jerusalem, the first step toward ‘all Judea’ (1:8).
passages.ot: God had promised through Moses that he would do wonders among his people, and Israel's story is told as a story of ‘signs and wonders’ in Egypt (Deuteronomy 4:34). Now, Luke says, the same God is doing signs and wonders through the apostles in Jerusalem, as Joel had foretold: “I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth” (Joel 2:30).
passages.asks: People were drawn and afraid at the same time. That is often how it is near God. Ask whether you have only known one side of it: a God who comforts, or a God to be feared. In Acts he is both, and people kept coming.

passages.t: Jailed, and set free by night
passages.happening:
The high priest and his associates, the party of the Sadducees, are filled with jealousy. They arrest the apostles and put them in the public jail.

“But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out” (verse 19), and tells them, “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life” (verse 20). At daybreak they are back in the temple, teaching.

The high priest calls the full council and sends for the prisoners. The officers come back puzzled: “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside” (verse 23). Then someone reports that the men are standing in the temple courts teaching the people. The captain and his officers bring them in, but not by force, “for fear the people would stone them” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
‘Jealousy’ is Luke's word for the leaders' motive. The apostles were winning the respect of the people, which the leaders thought belonged to them.

There is humour in this scene. The council sits in state and sends for the prisoners. The jail is locked, the guards are in place, and the cells are empty. Meanwhile the prisoners are a few hundred yards away doing exactly what they were jailed for.

The angel does not set them free so that they can escape to safety. He sends them straight back to the temple, the most public place in the city, to keep speaking. Their freedom is for the message, not for their comfort.

The leaders now fear the people. Only a few weeks earlier the leaders had stirred up a crowd against Jesus. Now the crowd is on the apostles' side.
passages.ot: God sending his angel to rescue his servants is an old story. Daniel, delivered from the lions, said, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions” (Daniel 6:22). A psalm promises, “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them” (Psalm 34:7).
passages.asks: The apostles were freed in order to go back to the very place that had got them arrested. Ask what you think God's help is for: to make your life easier, or to make you able to keep doing what he has given you to do. And notice the angel's words: ‘this new life’. That was the message, and it was worth the risk.

passages.t: ‘We must obey God rather than men’
passages.happening:
They stand the apostles before the council. The high priest says, “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name”, and goes on, “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood” (verse 28).

“But Peter and the other apostles replied, ‘We must obey God rather than men’” (verse 29). The God of their fathers raised up Jesus, whom the council had killed “by hanging Him on a tree” (verse 30). “God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel” (verse 31). “We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The high priest will not even say Jesus' name. He says ‘this name’ and ‘this man’.

He is afraid of being blamed for Jesus' death. Peter does not back away from the truth: the council did hand Jesus over. But again he holds out an offer. God exalted Jesus to give ‘repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel’. Even to the council that had condemned him, the door is open.

‘Prince’ is the same word Peter used for the ‘Author’ of life (3:15): a founder, a leader who goes first. ‘Savior’ is the one who rescues.

‘We must obey God rather than men’ repeats what Peter and John said at their first trial (4:19). The note on 4:13-22 explains why it is a refusal to stop speaking of Jesus, not a licence to disobey every rule, and how Christians differ on harder cases.
passages.ot: ‘Hanging Him on a tree’ is the language of the Law: “anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse” (Deuteronomy 21:23). By using those words, the apostles admit the scandal. To many Jews a crucified Messiah was a contradiction, since the Law called a man hanged on a tree cursed. The apostles answer that God has reversed the verdict by raising him. Paul later makes the same point: Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
passages.hard: ‘This man's blood’ and ‘whom you had killed’. As at 2:23, these are words between Jews in Jerusalem, spoken to the particular council that had handed Jesus over, about what that council did, and they come with an offer of forgiveness ‘to Israel’. They are not a verdict on the Jewish people. The note on 2:22-28 says more about how such verses were misused and why this site rejects that reading.
passages.asks: Peter told the most powerful men in Jerusalem both the hard truth and the open door in the same breath. Ask whether you can do both: say plainly what is wrong, and offer mercy in the same sentence. The gospel always does.

passages.t: Gamaliel's advice, a flogging, and joy
passages.happening:
The council members are furious and want to kill the apostles. “But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law who was honored by all the people, stood up in the Sanhedrin” (verse 34) and has the men put outside.

He reminds the council of two movements that failed. Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, with about four hundred men; he was killed and his followers scattered. After him, Judas the Galilean appeared “in the days of the census” and drew people after him; he too died and his followers scattered. “So in the present case I advise you: Leave these men alone” (verse 38). If this is of human origin, it will fail. “But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God” (verse 39).

The council agrees. They flog the apostles, order them again not to speak in Jesus' name, and let them go. “The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name” (verse 41). Every day, in the temple and from house to house, they keep teaching that Jesus is the Christ.
passages.hearers:
The Pharisees were the most popular of the Jewish groups. Unlike the Sadducees, they believed in the resurrection. Gamaliel was one of the most respected teachers of his day. Paul later says he was taught ‘at the feet of Gamaliel’ (22:3). Jewish tradition remembers a great teacher called Rabban Gamaliel the Elder; the Mishnah says that when he died, the glory of the law ceased. Most identify him with the Gamaliel of Acts.

Gamaliel is shown fairly and even warmly here. He does not believe in Jesus, but he is cautious and humble before God: he will not risk fighting against God. In later Christian speech ‘Pharisee’ came to mean a hypocrite, but Luke shows Pharisees who are wise (here), who warn Jesus of danger (Luke 13:31), and, later, who become believers (15:5).

Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6, when Judea came under direct Roman rule. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of him and of the movement that followed, which held that God alone was Israel's master.

The flogging was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes; Paul says he received it five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). It was painful and shaming. The apostles count the shame an honour, because it was ‘for the Name’.
passages.ot:
The Law limited a flogging: “He may receive no more than forty lashes” (Deuteronomy 25:3). Later Jewish practice, set down in the Mishnah, gave thirty-nine, to be sure not to go over the limit; Paul calls it “the forty lashes minus one” (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Gamaliel's warning about fighting against God has deep roots in Scripture. The wise men of Israel taught that “There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30).
passages.hard:
Gamaliel says Theudas came before Judas the Galilean, who rose up in AD 6. But Josephus tells of a Theudas who led a crowd to the Jordan, promising to part the river, and was killed under the Roman governor Fadus, around AD 44 to 46. That is about ten years after Gamaliel's speech, and long after Judas. The difficulty is real, and honest readers name it.

Several answers have been given. Some scholars think Luke made a mistake about the order or the date. Others think Gamaliel meant an earlier Theudas: it was a common name, and Josephus tells of many uprisings after Herod the Great died in 4 BC without naming every leader. Some have suggested that Luke misread Josephus, who tells of Theudas and then of the sons of Judas the Galilean; others answer that Josephus's book came out around AD 93, perhaps after Acts, and doubt that Luke used it. A few think Josephus himself has the order or the date wrong.

These notes do not settle it. The question is about the order of two failed rebels. It does not change Gamaliel's point, which history has borne out in a way he could not have guessed.
passages.asks: They were beaten and they went away rejoicing. Ask what it would take for you to count it an honour to be mocked or set back for following Jesus. Jesus had said, “Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven” (Matthew 5:12). And think about Gamaliel's test. Some things fade on their own; some things cannot be stopped. Ask which this has been.
